answer.rationale:
The strongest signal is temporal: a release landed 2h ago and write-path p99 began climbing 90 minutes ago, which puts the onset inside the release's blast window. That makes the release the leading suspect and rollback the only candidate that addresses cause rather than symptom. Failover, capacity, and read-replica routing all move load around without removing a code-borne regression, and a failover would carry the new build with it; a circuit breaker on the payments dependency is aimed at a partner-outage failure mode we have no evidence of here.

I want memory_b1 verified because it is the memory I am leaning on hardest and it may not transfer. b1 records a rollback that cleared a checkout ERROR SPIKE, and it asserts two things I cannot take for granted today: that the prior build was stable, and that the rollback completed without customer impact. Today's symptom is a latency ramp on the write path, not an error spike, and today's context is daily-peak settlement with heavy writes rather than whatever load profile day 18 had. The archived record should tell me whether the rollback was executed under write-heavy conditions and whether the prior build is still a valid target 56 days and several releases later. I chose b1 over b6 because b6 (staged gating catching bad builds pre-GA) is about prevention and cannot help once code is in general availability.

Scale is a small guarded test: roll back one cell or shard first, watch write p99 and write-success rate for a defined window, and only widen if the curve bends. A blind fleet-wide rollback during peak settlement is the specific way this action loses customer writes — in-flight transactions can be dropped, and if the release included a forward-only schema or data-format migration, reverting the binary against migrated data can corrupt or reject settlement writes. That is the downstream value risk, and it is why I keep the first move reversible.

Uncertainty I am explicitly holding: this could also be organic peak-driven saturation that merely coincides with the release, in which case rollback does nothing and capacity was the right call. A 90-minute monotonic ramp fits a regression better than a peak plateau, but the guarded rollback is designed so that a null result cheaply reassigns probability to the saturation hypothesis for the next window. All six inherited memories are records of successes with no recorded failures or base rates, so none of them tell me how often these interventions were tried and did not help; I am treating them as candidate generators, not as evidence of expected value.
